newsitem.title: USA: Time Warner to slim down after Turner merger.
newsitem.headline: Time Warner to slim down after Turner merger.

text.p: Time Warner Inc. was to formally take control of Turner Broadcasting System Inc. Thursday in a $6.7 billion transaction creating the world's biggest media group, which was likely to start quickly slimming down.
Time Warner shareholders voted early Thursday to approve the deal. By a preliminary accounting, 98.23 percent of shareholders approved the merger.
Shareholders of Turner Broadcasting were expected to approve the deal at a special afternoon meeting and the formal closing would follow shortly, the companies said.

Executives of the combined company, including Turner Broadcasting founder Ted Turner, who will be the largest individual shareholder in Time Warner, have been privately telling institutional investors that cost cuts will be coming and Time Warner's flamboyant spending history ended.
Time Warner Chairman Gerald Levin said Wednesday that planned cost-cutting would save the combined company some $600 million a year, according to people who attended an investors meeting.
The company also has reportedly hired consultants McKinsey & Co. to scour Time Warner for savings.
A Time Warner spokesman declined to comment.

Time Warner was also expected to resurrect efforts to pull back from owning and operating cable television systems, a capital-intensive business that accounts for much of the company's $17.5 billion in debt.
Turner, who will be vice chairman of Time Warner, told the investors meeting that he wants the company's debt halved.
His remarks prompted speculation that Time Warner, the second largest U.S. operator of cable systems, will spin off at least some of those operations.

Time Warner is a partner with U S West Media in many cable operations and is likely to seek a restructuring of that alliance, executives and analysts have said. U S West Media sued Time Warner when it announced its acquisition of Turner, but a Delaware judge earlier this year ruled against U S West.

"Everyone's on the same page on this," said Gordon Crawford, a fund manager at Capital Research Group, a major shareholder in both Time Warner and Turner Broadcasting. "Nobody wants $17 billion to $19 billion in debts at the end of the day."
Debt payments creating year after year of net losses have long overshadowed Time Warner's exceptionally strong operating performance, keepings its share price down, analysts have said.
Some cuts already have been announced at Turner Broadcasting, including a video-marketing operation made redundant by the merger -- even though it employs one of Ted Turner's children.
In addition, Atlantic Group, a recording division of Time Warner, announced Wednesday job cuts of as much as 13 percent of its 500 staff.
Time Warner shares gained 50 cents to $41.625 on the New York Stock Exchange, while Turner's shares added 25 cents to $31 on the American Stock Exchange.
